summary: ASTRA is a local network astronaut AI medical assistant that helps NASA analyze each astronaut’s physiological condition and mental health during mission. The website has a main overview which connects to the spacecraft monitoring systems. Each astronaut logs to their own account, where they’ll be able to see an overview of spacecraft condition and their physiological condition, inputted from Canadian Space Agency Bio-Monitor. Data from Canadian Active Neutron Spectrometer, is taken by ASTRA to detect the amount of radiation in the spacecraft. ASTRA takes input from astronauts on what they ate, with the food supply taken into account. A fitness tracker takes data from the Canadian Space Agency Bio-Monitor that automatically graphs the amount of exercise done. All this data tab has a built in local AI that analyzes the data and gives an accurate assessment. ASTRA will then give further instruction to help further decision making. This is important when you’re in space, astronauts aren’t able to contact and have to rely on training to diagnose their current health conditions. ASTRA acts as both a UNIFIED dashboard to monitor health from multiple sources, and an AI assistant to give assessment to each astronaut’s health and wellbeing.
details:
ASTRA is a medical decision-support prototype for astronauts on isolated, long-duration missions, where a ground flight surgeon can be 20+ light-minutes away. The crew member reports a concern in a chat consultation; ASTRA immediately runs a deterministic triage engine that returns red/yellow/green urgency, retrieves relevant background from a curated NASA Human Research Program corpus, and asks a grounded LLM to explain the concern using only those references. Meanwhile, a continuous vitals telemetry layer simulates a 10-metric physiology stream per crew member (heart rate, HRV, SpO₂, core temperature, blood pressure, sleep, radiation dose rate, cabin CO₂, stress index) with threshold bands and an alert lifecycle (open → acknowledge → auto-resolve on recovery). Both systems feed the same triage: live telemetry can escalate a consultation but never downgrade it. Incidents are persisted, restorable, and auditable. A 4D body-scan visualization, daily check-ins, nutrition/radiation tabs, and a three-press SOS flow complete the crew-facing dashboard.

Benefits. (1) Safety by construction: the LLM never owns urgency  a rule engine does, red emergencies skip generation entirely, and a safety guard runs on every response so model text can never soften an escalation. (2) Always available: if the provider fails or no key is configured, ASTRA falls back to deterministic responses labeled as such it never silently pretends to work. (3) Grounded answers: citations are traced to a versioned reference corpus; the model cannot invent sources. (4) Continuous monitoring: threshold alerts catch deterioration between consultations, the way a real crew medical officer watches trends.

The intended impact is to demonstrate a viable pattern for AI-assisted autonomous medical care in deep space: astronauts get immediate, structured, source-grounded guidance while the system preserves  and reinforces  the authority of human medical officers. Every output is validated : false and defers final decisions to the CMO and ground surgeon; the goal is a trustworthy decision-support layer, not an autonomous doctor. The architecture (deterministic-first triage, retrieval grounding, escalation-only telemetry coupling) is a reusable blueprint for high-stakes AI where a wrong "reassurance" is the worst failure mode.

Tools & stack. One TypeScript application: Next.js 16 (App Router) + React 19 + Tailwind CSS v4, backend as route handlers, persistence in SQLite via better-sqlite3 (with a production-shaped PostgreSQL/Supabase schema documented), LLM kimi-k3.1-pro through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint with graceful fallback, tests via Node's built-in node:test (74 passing, zero test deps), Git/GitHub with fork-and-PR collaboration, developed on Windows 11 (Node 24, VS 2022 Build Tools for native modules). UI designed from a Figma board.

A lazy vitals simulator that advances a seeded random-walk physiology model on read (no daemon needed inside serverless-style route handlers) and can inject scripted mission incidents solar particle events, CO₂ scrubber faults, post-EVA stress, sleep debt, febrile illness so the whole alert→triage→consultation chain can be demonstrated on demand; the worst-of triage merge that makes telemetry and conversation two independent deterministic rules that can only escalate each other; and a fully offline-capable medical assistant whose intelligence degrades honestly rather than failing.

Factors the team considered. Safety over capability  deterministic rules outrank the model at every layer, and all data/rules are labeled illustrative and non-clinical. Latency red emergencies return instantly without a network call. Failure modes provider outages fall back visibly; malformed history can never block opening a conversation. Trust every triage carries its rule ID and validated: false; references are versioned for traceability. Privacy & scope all crew data is fictional/simulated, there is no real authentication, and the prototype explicitly is not a medical device.
